title: Dry-run: message delivery and sync
intro: About 6 minutes. The defining constraint is that the server has to speak first — everything here follows from that, including why the servers can't be stateless.

steps.title: Name the constraint before designing
steps.explain: Almost everything else you design is request/response. Chat is server-initiated: a message arrives for you and the system must push it to a device that is not asking for anything. Saying this first frames every decision that follows.
steps.saysOutLoud: The server has to initiate, so I need a persistent connection — that makes the tier stateful.

steps.title: A registry maps user to server
steps.explain: Because connections are stateful, delivering a message means first discovering which machine holds the recipient's socket. The TTL is the important detail — connections die without a close frame when a phone loses signal, so entries must expire on their own.

steps.title: Persist before delivering
steps.explain: Store the message and assign a server-side ordering id first. Persisting before delivery is what makes the message survive a crash mid-send — and the id must come from the server because device clocks disagree, drift, and can be set by the user.
steps.saysOutLoud: Server-assigned id, never the client's clock — otherwise messages appear out of order.

steps.title: Deliver via the registry, with one internal hop
steps.explain: Look up each recipient's server and forward. If there is no live entry the message is already durable in the conversation, so nothing is lost — you just trigger a mobile push as a side channel instead.

steps.title: Per-device cursors do all the sync work
steps.explain: This is the idea worth landing. One mechanism covers first sync, catch-up after a week offline, and recovery from a two-second blip — there is no special case for any of them, which is why it is worth choosing deliberately.
steps.saysOutLoud: A cursor per device. A two-second blip and a two-week absence take the same path.

steps.title: Storage is partitioned by conversation
steps.explain: A wide-column store partitioned by conversation and clustered by message id puts the newest messages physically contiguous, so fetching a screenful is one sequential read and scrolling back continues along the same partition. Add a time bucket to the partition key so a group chat running for years does not grow one partition without bound.

steps.title: At-least-once plus idempotency, not exactly-once
steps.explain: Networks drop acknowledgements, so clients retry and the server may see the same message twice. The client-generated key makes the repeat a no-op — that is how you get exactly-once behaviour without claiming a guarantee you cannot provide.

steps.title: Group fan-out inverts above a cap
steps.explain: For a capped group, delivery is a loop — which is why the cap exists. Above that, per-message fan-out stops being viable and you store once and let clients pull, which is the same trade as the news feed and worth naming as such.

steps.title: Plan for the reconnect storm
steps.explain: Restarting a connection server drops every socket it holds and they all reconnect at once. Drain before shutdown and require jittered client backoff — without jitter the fleet synchronises and knocks the server over again as it comes back.
steps.saysOutLoud: Deploys drop thousands of sockets at once, so drain first and jitter the reconnects.

closing: If they raise end-to-end encryption: say plainly what it costs — the server can no longer read content, so server-side search, previews and moderation move to the client, and multi-device sync gets substantially harder because each device needs its own key material.
